moments.topic: THE INSTRUCTOR KNEW HIM FROM A DRIFT VIDEO
moments.quote: when you jump from the plane and your head is not like right away facing down, you're just like, where am I? And you know, your, your heart kind of stays into the plane and your body jumps down. It's kind of a special feeling, very nice feeling. But, uh, like once I was like, all right, I see the ground. Like it was, it was just, okay. I was like, all right, let's maybe do it again. Or when we opened up the, the, the, the thing, you know, the parachute, the parachute, I was, I was telling the guy, you know, can we do some, you know, like backflips and stuff. And he actually knew me from a video that I did in, in Quebec, uh, about drifting and the stunts grabbing, you know? So he was like, uh, he was like, hello, man, let's do it.
moments.why: Asked for flips under the parachute; the instructor knew him from a Quebec drift video.

moments.quote: But for me being in this situation, I kind of feel sometimes like I don't live things at the right level of emotion that should. Interesting. Okay. And my girlfriends tell me that sometimes she's like, you will live something crazy, like skydiving and you'll be like, that was nice. Yeah. Very nice. And you will be very sad. And I'll be like, Oh, yeah, I'm kind of sad. And well, I won't cry, you know, and she's like normal people. We, well, not normal people, but other people, they, they will live a high emotion and it will be a lot, you know, it will be like crazy or they will fear it too much, or it will be sad or happy or whatever. For, for me, I feel like it's more like neutral all the time. And I need this adrenaline feel a little bit more, you know, something I will say, but it is, it's never really enough.
moments.why: He feels emotions on a neutral level and keeps chasing adrenaline. Honest moment.

moments.topic: HE PRACTISES HIS RUNS IN THE SAUNA
moments.quote: when I'm in the sona, I always visualize my run in my head while I work on my, uh, my breathing. So I breathe and I try to do the run and, you know, work with my pedal and work with my handbrake at the same time. And it helps me being more focused and being more connected to, uh, the car when I'm in the car or my buddy when I'm in the soda. See what I mean? So it's a little bit more spirit spiritual, but, uh, for me, for me, it works because I feel like we're all very good drivers. You know, we are all able to put the car right on the line. We are all champions from where we are coming from. So I'm trying to find what makes a difference. And the more I work on my driving career, the more I realize that the biggest difference comes with in the mental side of things.
moments.why: Visualises runs, pedals and handbrake while doing breath work in the sauna.

moments.quote: this, this season, I'm not going to drink a single beer just to know, to, you know, get more serious, be more focused or whatever. And it didn't really work. And after that, I changed my, my perception of things. And I was like, all right, maybe what I did is that I tried to make this whole thing way too serious. And I put more pressure on myself doing this. And by putting more pressure to my, on myself, I put more stress and it affect my result on the track. So after that, I was like, all right, let's not be a hungover. But I was like, if I want to, if I feel like I want to have a beer, like after the race or like, you know, after qualifying, because we did, we did a good qualifying, I will have one and I will see it as like, well, you know what, it's all a game. It's all, it's all for fun. And this reduce the amount of pressure I put on myself and reduce the amount of stress and it, it, it makes my driving looks better.
moments.why: Went a whole Pro Spec season without a beer to be serious; more pressure, worse results.

moments.topic: FACING JAMES DOES NOT CHANGE ANYTHING
moments.quote: So let's say I go against James, which is probably the greatest driver in the world right now. Or I go against another guy. It won't, it won't really change the way I still run. And sometimes people are like, Oh, you're going against like one of the best driver in the world. Like how do you feel? Well, that's where I go back to like, well, good. I mean, you know, it's kind of the driver and you see where the, you know, the, it goes back to what we talked earlier. So, but yeah, for sure. I want to enjoy it because I know that I am lucky to be here and at any time it could stop. So I'm trying to take it in and enjoy it. But when the lights go like green and I pulled, I pulled down the visor, it's just like, you could be any other driver. It won't, it won't really affect my stress level because, because, because if it affects it, well, I will be, I will lose the battle before we even started.
moments.why: Even against James, whom he calls the best driver in the world right now, his stress stays the same.

moments.topic: TOMMY AS DRIVER LIAISON NEXT YEAR?
moments.quote: Okay. So let's say, let's say the, the, the entire grid deems you as a new driver liaison representative. What would you fight for to change when it comes to the series? Is there something that you want to see different? We've talked about points a little bit, but is there something that, cause there's, there's actually a good chance that you could become driver liaison next year. I don't know if that's something you've thought about or wanted to do, but is there something you would like to see updated for next year season?
moments.why: The host says there is a good chance Tommy becomes FD driver liaison next year. Rumor, needs Joshua.

moments.topic: WHY DO DRIVERS PAY TO RACE FD?
moments.quote: I always feel like who's putting on a show is the drivers who's like putting their, their life on buzz for this series is the drivers who is like the talent is the drivers. So I still don't understand why is the drivers that has to pay to get there, you know, in the, in the series and most of the other series, they, they are paid to go there. And for us in the former group, which is the highest level of drifting in the world, we are still needing to pay for our entrance for me. It doesn't really make sense.
moments.why: Drivers put on the show and risk their lives but still pay entry. Discussion starter.

moments.topic: NASCAR FRIENDS GET PAID TO SHOW UP
moments.quote: I have some friends that are, you know, running in a NASCAR or other professional series and they're like, yeah, well, we, we, we received like 200 bucks to get to the track. I'm like, Oh, that's, that's not a lot, but they're like, yeah, but how much do you pay? Like, Oh yeah, I pay like a lot to get to the track. You know, so I'm like, yeah, it just makes sense. And they say like, yeah, but look in the, in the grass stands there, there's like 15 ,000 people coming to see us and who's taking the money from that, the series. So it's just normal that the Siri pay us. And I'm like, Oh, well that makes sense.
moments.why: His friends in other series get paid to show up; in FD drivers pay.

moments.quote: Have you, have you tried to like talk to anybody at like Chevrolet Canada or anything? Yeah. Yeah, I did. And it was never a big success. And I didn't try on the US side, but I, I didn't try also because I know that Matt did try and still trying. Yeah. Well, that makes sense. I was to try if I was in and I know that it's not a big success for now. So I'm like, all right. Well, that's this, there's that. It's kind of happened eventually though. Like it has towards involved Toyota's involved. Nissan. You know, we've had Nissan involved. Yeah. Like why not? Why not Chevrolet? Yeah. That would just make sense. And like 80% of the field run like Chevrolet and GM engines.
moments.why: Tommy tried Chevrolet Canada; says Matt is still trying with Chevrolet. Rumor, needs Joshua.

episodes.title: OEM+ vs. Custom Builds: What’s the BEST Way to Build a Car?

moments.quote: I think OEM plus is a tough one because that's that's a term that gets sort of like sort of the lines get blurred, sort of like how JDM became such a blurred line, you know, years and years ago. It went from something that was very, very specific and very, you know, very to the point. And then it sort of got got muddied up and it went all over the place. And you go on on eBay or something and everything is everything is JDM, right? Facebook Marketplace, everything's JDM. I mean, we're guilty of it here, too. I mean, we throw that term around and you and I both know that that's not how the term was used, but we throw it around just like it's, you know, a regular run of the mill car is JDM. Yeah, I think I knew it was bad in the early days when people at my at my job, this is one of the much younger were like, hey, is that your JDM out there? And I was like, what are you talking about? They were just talking about I just had a civic it was modified. But yeah, or a CRX. I'm sorry. But that's when I realized, oh, man, this term really went out there.
moments.why: Why JDM and OEM+ became meaningless buzzwords, with a funny workplace story.

moments.quote: and I feel like at times it does get a little bit lazy with OEM plus stuff, because it's like, it's sort of like this proven formula that you know, will work if you've got, you know, a white 96 Civic and you're putting a bunch of Type R stuff on it from, you know, from the, from the UK nine. You already know what it's going to look like, right? Because there's a ton of them out there or you're putting the same exact parts that the other 30 guys in the next town over have on their white 96 Civic. I understand the appeal because it looks really, really good, but it's been done so many times before there's got to be a point where you're like, man, it's just, it's a clone, but there's so many that live exactly the same. So I do feel like at times that OEM plus stuff does get a little bit lazy. Um, but that's coming from someone that likes to modify. I like to tinker, I like to play with the car and change stuff up. So for me, if I was going to build something like that, it would be cool for a little bit, but then I'd have to, I have to do more of the plus side, like really start bringing in, uh, some market goods, cause I just get bored.
moments.why: Hot take that OEM+ builds are a copy-paste formula, sure to divide Honda fans.

moments.quote: I think the confusion is when you see a company like Nukem that's so closely related to Honda, a lot of people, especially the newer crowd, they think that those are actual Honda products. It's OEM stuff. It's not. It's an aftermarket brand, right? That company, especially, was so focused on motorsport products for so many years and they did so well. But in more recent years, you see a lot of that stuff they're making is just for like streetcars, right? So like floor mats and window visors. And I think they even have like a little protector that goes behind the door handle so your key doesn't scratch it. So there's all these little things they make, right? The little knickknacks and stuff. So you see them sort of transitioning, still making performance products, but also going into that realm as well. That stuff again, in my opinion, it's not OEM plus. That's aftermarket goods.
moments.why: Clears up a common myth: Mugen parts are aftermarket, not factory Honda.

moments.quote: Am I, on my VQ 37, I'm putting the GTR twin turbos on it because of, you know, fitment, it's the best setup I can do. But there's other companies that make great twin turbo kits that would be a much better option if it was in stock chassis and all that. But my point being like, there are way better aftermarket solutions than what the OE offers in that instance. So am I shooting myself in the foot and setting myself up to fail by saying, okay, I'm going to stay in this, you know, box and not do anything outside of it? Or do I just go for what's best and what's the best opportunity for me to build something? Yeah, I mean, it's your money, right? You have to decide what, how it's going to work for you, where you want to put it, because you don't get it back, right?
moments.why: Host reveals his VQ37 build uses GT-R twin turbos and questions sticking to OEM.

moments.topic: COLD AIR INTAKES DON'T MAKE POWER
moments.quote: And, you know, I've seen it firsthand cold air intakes and you know, as well as I do, do not make power. They're not, you know, putting a cold air intake does not necessarily mean that you're going to gain horsepower. You might gain a little bit of feel. It might move the power band around, depending on, you know, flow diameter of the pipe and things like that. Fine. But there's something to be said about a team of engineers that set out to make that, say that manifold, that exhaust manifold flow as efficiently as possible and to work as well as it does into obviously fit. They put a lot of time and effort into the fit and finish and how it's going to fit on the vehicle. And I think that's where we really see that shine through now.
moments.why: Bold claim against a classic first mod, backed by praise for factory engineering.

moments.quote: If not, wiring specialties just recently announced that they're doing a VR 30 swap kit for the Z33 chassis for the 350Z chassis. I think it is brilliant. Like genuinely, I think that it's very smart to keep the longevity of both of the platforms going. Like, yes, the VR 30 has its issues and everyone can complain. But yet again, a junkyard motor capable of 400 horsepower. Like, let's just, you know, lay that out there and going into a, you know, an O3, O4, 350Z platform, it's a super light chassis for that. And it's gonna and they're getting cheap. You know, let's be honest, the G35 and 350Z have come down significantly. So if you know, for one with a blown engine or anything like that, you can get a chassis. I'm saying for a decent price.
moments.why: Wiring Specialties VR30 swap kit for Z33: big news for budget drift chassis builders.

moments.quote: You know, I should say, it sounds like I'm sort of hating on OEM plus built. I'm definitely not. I did one for a little while. And like I said, you know, I got bored and I moved on. A little while. I didn't want a necessity at the time I was very young. And I may or may not have been charged for multiple counts of street racing and whatever. And then I had purchased a vehicle and I decided to put an engine in it. A lot of the vehicle stock, put a different Honda engine in it. Different OEM wheels and a lip from a higher model. I cruised that around for a while. And that was just what I had. And it was definitely OEM plus. And, you know, it worked for me, but eventually moved on.
moments.why: Funny confession: multiple street racing charges led to a quiet OEM+ Honda.

moments.quote: That ultimately led, especially in like the Honda and Nissan world, to a lot of theft. And I think it's, you know, it's pretty well known. Type Rs were constantly getting stolen. GSRs, you know, losing their engine transmission, wheels, brakes, seats, all that kind of stuff. So it definitely had a negative impact, but it was also a positive one because it got everybody modified and going nuts with building cars, you know. Especially we're talking, you know, like late 90s, early 2000s. I mean, it was insane how many people had built coming out. So, you know, there's the good and the bad, right? Because it definitely led to a lot more theft because people wanted to get those parts and they weren't willing to buy them. So there's a problem.
moments.why: How the hunt for higher-trim parts fuelled the late 90s Type R and GSR theft wave.

moments.quote: But even a junkyard cast iron 5 .3 liter can make 500 horsepower with the right setup in it. And you don't have that with a civic, let's say, like you're not, you're not going to be able to run out there and make a natural aspirated civic, make 500 horsepower. Like that's not a normal thing. And you're not going to probably be wanting to drive it once it is making 500 natural, natural aspirated horsepower. It's going to be quite a handful. I'm sure. So my, the thing that I think is that was always just the chase of how to make quick power, how to make it cheap. How to have a fast car. It was never about, hey, I need this part because it makes the car more like the higher trim level. You know, nobody was putting a Hellcat motor in their scat pack to make it a Hellcat. They were just doing it to have a fast scat pack.
moments.why: Domestic vs import: a junkyard LS makes 500 hp, a Civic never will.

moments.quote: That's the same thing with the Volkswagen crowd. And I think even the Corvette crowd too, right? Like the Corvette guys are like that way too, you know, that I don't, I don't know anything about high socks, new balances and tan shorts. I'm just saying they could all catch strays. It's okay. You know me, I have much more. I'll take my, my problems circled, you know, nice little Ford logo or the Nissan one. They circle my problems. I already know what I have. Don't worry.
moments.why: Lighthearted roast of Corvette owners, then a self-own about Ford and Nissan.

moments.quote: So for me, to see Audi parts on a Volkswagen is not uncommon. You know, to see, you know, S3 parts on a Jetta or what I don't know how it exactly works. But my point being to see those crossovers, not that big of a deal, where I start to have the issue is where it's like, oh, but for instance, we talked about it when we're talking about the OEM wheels. Check out that podcast if you haven't. I had Mustang wheels on my Nissan. To me, that's not OEM plus, even if it's a Mustang wheel off of a OEM car, because we've now switched genres, let's say, to me, or, you know, switch manufacturers, it's a completely no longer the case. It's always been that DNA, that continuation of the brand, makes it the OEM plus as in they've made the car better than what the manufacturer could by using the main or what the manufacturer could have made the car to be by using manufacturer parts. I guess is the way that I define it.
moments.why: A clear rule: OEM+ means parts from the same brand family, Mustang wheels on a Nissan don't count.

moments.topic: THE WING THAT BROKE THE INTERNET
moments.quote: On the outside of the car though, completely all Accord Euro R stuff, except for a big wing, because he didn't track the car once in a while, right? And then obviously aftermarket wheels. So in essence, I should not have been really called an OEM plus build. However, see to me, it's not. However, the rider, because he's just so smart, decided to call it an OEM plus build. And I mean, you call it a little bit of clickbait, I guess. But, you know, I basically kind of put in there that it was an OEM plus sort of build. And it caused - Plus plus build, OEM plus plus plus build. I think I actually said that in the end. But it's funny because it brought up a lot of commentary and it did its job as far as traffic, because people wanted to comment on it and say, you know, this or that. But it's funny because of all the posts that came up about it, like 95 % were all, how is OEM plus if it has that big wing in the back? Forget the brakes, the wheels, the suspension. All the bushing, all the stuff he did under, you know, all the stuff underneath, he had aftermarket seats, he had shifter, steering wheel, all the stuff, supercharged, it had her. The whole thing, right? So he had all the stuff done to it, but all anybody could focus on was the big wing.
moments.why: Story of an Acura TSX called OEM+ where commenters only cared about the wing.

episodes.title: Christian Cotrone

moments.topic: HIS HAPPY PLACE? OSW SKID PAD
moments.quote: Huge passion. I got to share with my dad growing up. Um, and to this day, man, like, uh, if you tell me like, where is your happy place, like I'm not going to tell you like a beach or a Bahamas, like I will tell you like the OSW skid pad, like it's just, you know, it's where I am comfortable is where I enjoy my time. And it's just being at the track, uh, the relationships we build out there as well. Um, I just, I love it, man.
moments.why: Cotrone picks a Florida skid pad over any beach, pure grassroots love.

moments.quote: yeah, I don't think I've missed the black Friday since I started driving. So this would probably be like my seventh or eighth year. Um, but it's been a while. It's I think I last time I won, it was in 21. There's definitely been a lot more changes, a lot more money involved now. But I don't know. It's like, I was talking to my wife about it, uh, about black Friday and she's like, you're not going to bring the Corvette. Are you? And I was like, ah, you know, there's, there's a lot of money on the line, but she's like, that's like, that's a lose lose. Because if you get the, you look like a dumbass, you're someone in their stock through DC and then if you win, they're just gonna go, Oh, you brought his pro car. You know, so it's, it's, I feel like it's very much so like a lose lose, but, uh, we'll see what we show up with.
moments.why: His wife calls bringing the FD Corvette to a grassroots event a lose-lose.

moments.quote: I was really, really fortunate for my first car. Uh, my uncle had like a few cars, a collection of cars, essentially. He was a big Camaro guy. Oh, so he had a replica SS 94 Z 28 Camaro and I had like 60 ,000 miles on it. And at that time it was probably, I don't know, 10, you know, like 10, 11 years old. So, you know, it had a low mileage and it just sat there. And so he basically was like, Hey, would you want to take this as your first car? It was in Pennsylvania. Um, and I just worked essentially for those two years straight to have enough money to get that car and then, uh, got to start with a, unfortunately it was automatic, but it was a Z 28. We're going to drive LT one. I had a little cul -de -sac at the end of my road and I would just do donuts, man. And that thing, that was a just power slide, you know, and just get that thing sideways, uh, always was obsessed with that.
moments.why: His drifting started with donuts in an automatic Camaro Z28 in a cul-de-sac.

moments.quote: it was cool because I actually got my first job at a Nissan dealership. So at 15, I started working at a Nissan dealership, um, and worked there for a few years and that was, uh, 2005. So that was at the time, like the Z just came out in no three. So I got to just drool over through the Z work on them. I was like the guy that would, uh, if you bought a new car, I'd go like, fill it up with gas and drop it off the detail and then like, bring it to them so they can basically give you the new car. So I got to like drive all these cool cars, like ETR, some used cars. Um, so yeah, man, I just kind of worked really hard and I was able to work out a deal for a three, three 50 Z, uh, brand new when I was like 17 years old. Nice. Yeah. So it was just like a, um, uh, employee discount financed it.
moments.why: He worked at a Nissan dealer from age 15 and bought a brand new 350Z at 17.

moments.quote: And I'm a big Corvette guy. I think the best looking car out there, of course. Uh, and, uh, we jumped into that platform at the time where there was like zero aftermarket support, uh, around COVID. And there was, uh, just a bunch of cars for sale at the time because I think there was no aftermarket support. So it wasn't really a hyped up car at the time. So we got to essentially Trey. I traded like a three of the Z and a G 35 and, uh, was able to trade, um, directly for the Corvette. So I have a crazy story on that. I literally think like we're, I got into the Corvette, like sub $2 ,000.
moments.why: He traded a 350Z and a G35 for the Corvette and paid under 2,000 dollars on top.

moments.quote: And so once we built the car, uh, both the car, it was essentially a stock motor with angle kit and the right arms and parts and going out there and swinging, uh, at clutch triggers. And I'm sure you remember, man, that was when it went over to fetuses over at freedom factory. It's just like unlimited. You can run a, you know, three 15, whatever, you know, Ron would do bro and whatever, uh, so I was out there with the 400 horsepower car. I'm going up against, you know, fully built pro one guys. Uh, but I loved it, man. Like I loved the whole process of learning, um, and just, you know, growing at in the competitive drifting scene. I remember just like still going to those events and like, we're going to be on the podium, like still having that mindset, like right out the gate. And then just getting completely smashed by, you know, a thousand horsepower. Like I remember going to, I want to again, it's like Jonathan near and his crazy car. And he just dored me. Like I just, and I couldn't keep up with him and dored me. I never called my wife after. And I was just like, man, just like bomb. She's like, what do you expect?
moments.why: His first comps were a 400 hp Corvette against fully built pro cars, and he got smashed.

moments.quote: And so in 24, we went out there swinging, um, and just dealt with, um, not so much mechanical, uh, just like. Just issues with other drivers. Honestly, like we got hit a ton the first year and we just had, um, just things break that kind of put us out of that top spot. I think that first year we ended up at like, um, like a fifth or a sixth position. So, um, wasn't the best. Um, and then coming into 25, um, the car was dialed. Everything was ready to go. We did. There wasn't like a learning curve or anything like that. Um, and we just kind of set out to make it happen in 25. And it was a super successful year. I think, uh, we ended up podium, like, I think three out of the four rounds, uh, multiple first places. I think we won it by like 200 points.
moments.why: After a rough first Pro-Am year he won USDC in 2025 by about 200 points.

moments.quote: Evan over at lead foot and Achilles, uh, their, their buddies of mine. So I've always helped out anytime I can with them. They reached out originally and they, me and Dan and, and Shulman went out there and did some initial testing for them. So Achilles always calling my line. He's like, what do you think about this? What do you think about that? Evan, his son has been doing amazing on to the promotion side of things. Socials have been out there. That's all him. So shout out to Evan. So yeah, they've been kind of giving me the sneak peeks of what they got, you know, going, so I'm excited. Uh, and now we just need about two more of those throughout the state. And it will be in a good spot.
moments.why: He helped test Lead Foot, a new Florida drift venue, and wants two more in the state.

moments.quote: So I know there's a lot, you know, that they have tried. Um, and I've even seen, um, you know, a mock -up of the actual, they want to build a track behind the skit pad, like an actual roof course. I've seen the plans for that for six, seven years, you know, like, yeah, I know it's there, um, and it's just kind of on them and just having all those stars align and of course the, the track owner being on board on that side. Cause I know they make a ton of money on the drag side. So it's just kind of like, what do we need to invest into the drifting? If we don't see the return at the end of the day, uh, again, it's just, you know, as a business owner, I see all the sides, but the drifter in me is just like, let's just fricking pave that thing.
moments.why: He has seen plans for a road course behind the OSW skid pad for six or seven years.

moments.quote: We've been super fortunate just with the amount of practice in the rain. And that's why like anytime in FD, when it ran, I was go, because I know, especially on these banks and these old rules, man, like I love driving in the rain on the old, like it's not a bank done deal. I'm like out there doing the rain dance, you know, like I'm like, what let it rain. Especially because we dealt with a ton of motor issues and power delivery issues this year. I was like, man, if it rains, we all got a thousand horsepower.
moments.why: With engine trouble all year, rain was his equalizer in FD.

moments.quote: It was, it was rough for us and it was like in my mind, like I'm like watching everything, you know, years prior, I'm like, man, why do all these guys come to the FD have all these changes and look like a fish out of water? I'm like, once we get our license, we will not do that. And then of course we get our license. I'm like, all right guys, we need more power. So we go and make all these upgrades to the motor. And then unfortunately it's just, this isn't the right recipe. And it's like, this is what we got to use. Um, and it's like, I literally just all year, man, I'm like, I wish we just kind of kept this setup we had in program. I just thought I was a little underpowered. Um, and unfortunately it's just the setup we went with this year. It just didn't give us the sauce we needed.
moments.why: He swore he would not change everything for FD, then chased power and lost his setup.

moments.quote: And it's just like going back to his crew, man. It's just, I remember watching just in Atlanta, the first round, like my crew was there with him and they had, um, impact and went into the wall. And, um, with Gucci, I think, I just remember them pulling the car apart, like it coming in and the work they did in five minutes. And one of my crew guys just looked at me and he goes, we got a lot of work to do just because of how dialed and like things come in. They don't even say anything. Like every single person knows their job. Every single person knows this is the tool. This is the size I need. Um, and that just takes years, man, of practice and really kind of going through the right setup, um, and just really learning everything in and out of the car and it just, it comes with experience. Um, and I was definitely humbled by just all of that.
moments.why: Seeing Matt Field's crew rebuild after a wall hit in five minutes humbled his team.

moments.quote: FDs, uh, it's, it's insane how, it's insane how different it is compared to even a pro -am series, right? Like, I think this year, um, there was only one round that we actually had more than four laps in practice. Wow. So yeah, I think Atlanta around one, we had two laps in practice. The first lap, the car over -rotated and went into the wall, uh, same wall. Matt hit my very first practice lap in FD. That's exactly how it went. So didn't start off so great. Uh, and then, um, it just kind of, you know, went downhill from there to be honest. It just, uh, it's just, uh, yeah, it was just rough this year. So we, uh, and you know, a lot of people are like, Oh, this is your rookie year. You got to expect that. But for me and my team, like we have very high expectations, right? And we were like, all right, this is where we're going to be. This is what we need. Uh, and we're going to execute and be on that podium.
moments.why: His first ever FD practice lap ended in the same wall Matt Field hit.

moments.quote: Like in pro -am I could literally, we have probably two, maybe three sessions, an hour and a half each. So like three, four and a half hours of practice. Um, and here, like I said, man, you're, you're lucky to get three, four laps. Um, with how many drivers are in prospect and site someone was in the wall and they're in, you lose 20 minutes. Um, and so, uh, I think Atlanta, yeah, we got two laps. Um, Connecticut, I think we got two laps. Um, Indy, we got, I think five laps. Um, and that was the only, um, event that we actually had success with the motor set up and just everything. And then last round, I think we got three laps.
moments.why: Pro-Am gave him hours of practice, FD PROSPEC gave him two to five laps.

moments.quote: and then as soon as I like knew, okay, we're probably gonna get our license, I'm gonna be like, I want to reach out and I want to work with someone next year. I really want to learn, of course, like I'm going to go ahead and learn from the Corvette master, right? And so, uh, just reaching out to him and I'm like, brother, like I see what you're doing on the marketing side. Um, and I think I can help you. And it's just very strict. That's a bold statement, right? Yeah. And I'm just like, listen, man, like this is what I essentially can offer you. And this is what we can do. Um, and I think that, you know, at first he was like, well, how are you different than the 60 other media guys that come out to every single event? And I'm like, brother, like we're going to go a completely different route for you.
moments.why: He pitched the Corvette master on marketing to earn his help in FD.

moments.quote: And I really kind of, uh, was taken back by how much he actually invested into me and my program. Like, it wasn't just like, cool, you're going to do this. We're going to help you out. It was very much so him checking me on me. Like, did you do this, do that? Like, what's the alignment currently? Um, and then when he came out to Orlando, he spent a bunch of time with me and the team going over the car, dialing in the car. So just going above and beyond. Uh, and it didn't feel like a transactional. It was very much so a personal, um, relationship with him. And, um, yeah, I just thank him for all the support, um, the guidance this year and just staying on me and just really exposing a lot of things that like changes that we need to make to be successful. Um, and he, he's tough on me, man. Like he'll tell me the truth. He'll be like, yeah, this, this isn't it. Or like, you got to do this. And then his mom and dad as well, like, yeah, they are, I, I'm so thankful for the relationship with them as well. Like his mom's like, yeah, you need to do this. You need to do that. She's like, these are the type of hero cards you need. Like all this and the merch.
moments.why: Matt Field and his parents mentored him hard, down to hero cards and merch.

moments.quote: You don't understand like the fire that's been lit under my butt matter for next year to do everything that we possibly can. Like the car was back from Vegas in two days. Like they already pulled the car apart already on plan a of like trying to get into the best spot for next year. So like we can test next month. Like we're not, we're not playing like we're like, all right, this is what's needed. These are the partners that we're focusing on. This is a setup we want to focus on and doing things like practicing five minute, you know, calls and changes. Oh, that's a good one. Man, like that's a good one. All that stuff. So we can pull up next year and we're like, yep, we're going to be a top contender and that's it.
moments.why: The car was torn down two days after Vegas, testing next month, aiming for top contender.

moments.quote: I remember telling my dad, Hey, I'm moving to LA and he's like, yeah, good luck with that. And I had $500 in my name, you know, and that was a jumping in to the scene. I think that Russian roulette video, I literally worked. It was an 18 hour a day and I got a $20 gas stipend. Damn. So it's like, people don't understand like the industry and like what you truly have to do to like get in the right position. Uh, and like, that's just an example, man. Like that was a short film and there, they probably had a budget of $5 ,000 total for this thing. And there was mainly all volunteers and it was like my first, uh, you know, I guess putting my toes in the water or whatever you want to call it, uh, on an actual film set.
moments.why: He moved to LA with 500 dollars and worked 18 hour days for a 20 dollar gas stipend.

moments.quote: So cool facts. The, I, when I moved out to LA, I worked for a DP at the time, director of photography, and he was the one that shot all Lincoln parks music videos. That's crazy. Small world. And Michael Jackson, he did a bunch of Mike, Michael Jackson music videos. And so I was basically his assistant. He was like, yeah, this is what you need to do to be successful. And I just remember like looking at his reels and like he worked for huge hubby Gucci, a Maserati Bentley, like all these high end brands. Um, and just seeing like his journey, but yeah, he did all Lincoln parks. That's cool videos and stuff like that. So yeah, shout out to Ross Richardson.
moments.why: His first LA mentor was the DP behind Linkin Park and Michael Jackson videos.

moments.quote: I think all it truly comes down to it was like, of course we want to always elevate. Right. Like we all want to come out next year, like swinging. Um, of course it just comes down to. Funding and getting the right partners involved. Um, and so we're definitely in that process. Like again, we just want to elevate it and put the right people in place, but there's some pretty big, uh, things brewing on the interclip side, uh, along with formula drift that, uh, uh, we can't say just yet, but things, things are bubbling, so we're really, we're really excited. Um, hopefully these things really kind of go through. Um, and we want to grow, like the whole point of the series is like a drive to survive type of series.
moments.why: He hints at something big brewing between Interclip and Formula DRIFT.

moments.quote: I think drifting needs it. I think it will help with, um, the fan base. I think F1 got a huge, uh, uptick in, you know, fans after all that came out. Cause then the day then you can be, you can relate to the drivers, you know, and you can see what they're going and dealing with. Um, you can see how they handle these situations. Um, and I think it's super powerful. It's just, we are, uh, we're slowly starting to see, you know, kind of a wave of some guys trying it as well. Right. The longer form type of content. And that was such a big thing where we had a pitch to Matt and Brandon of like, it's going to be long form. It's not going to be like the snappy stuff, but like the viewer count and the watch time like speaks for itself. Like these are 40 minute videos and people are watching, you know, 98 % of the video. Like it's, it's insane. And so kind of like that really speaks for itself. It shows us, Hey, there is a demand.
moments.why: Their 40 minute videos keep viewers for 98 percent of the runtime.

moments.quote: Matt's Matt's insane though. That man can riff off. And I'm like, Oh, just like, you know, partner bits of like, say this, say that. Like we just like tell him, and then he just like just nails it. I'm like, yeah, that's just like, and that comes with the experience, right? And all the years of doing that and being camera ready. Uh, but yeah, these interviews take a long time and just like the whole editing process, uh, the amount of time that Loxie will take for these edits. Uh, it's like a full week essentially. Um, and so it just takes a lot, um, from everything down to sound design for each and every clip and, and, and sinking of, uh, 12 cameras, you know, like everything is like time coded and go across the board so we can see what camera at what time, so we know we can pull it.
moments.why: Matt Field nails every line, but each edit takes a week with 12 synced cameras.

moments.quote: Uh, but they are, um, cooking up an episode that covers around two, three, and four of mine. So we have, of course, yeah. So we have the first round out in Atlanta, just kind of showcasing like how rough that round was, uh, and then we're going to have just like one big, uh, episode for myself here coming out in the next few weeks. So, uh, we're cranking out Matt's last round video and that should be going live this week and the weekend. So obviously on the podium. Uh, so we're super excited about that. Uh, I was just like, man, we got to get a win because no one wants to watch the same thing, dude blow the door up every round. And it's just like, we'll be back next round.
moments.why: An Interclip episode on his rounds two to four is coming, plus Matt Field's podium video.

moments.quote: Like we get to record all Matt's like teams comms. And so like, man, the editing on that has got to be wild. Oh my God. It's just, it's just funny. Cause like Jacob and Loxley, like they have, uh, you know, uh, ear whatever so they can hear everything just from their comms. Then we're recording that to basically and time coding that as well. And so we have all that, but man, like the stuff that they say and like how they just operate and flow throughout the day, it's like, I, you can listen to that stuff alone and it'd be like the best content ever. So it's just kind of going that extra level and, and, and that's the stuff that you're not going to hear or see anywhere else. Yeah. And so like having that and being like, this is what chow his spotters saying to him in this moment and stuff like that. Like he can be so brutal to Matt, like, but it's, it's, it works for them.
moments.why: They record Matt Field's team radio, and the spotter can be brutal.

moments.quote: Brother on top of that, I also, we had our second kid in between rounds two and three. Yeah. So I was told, I was like asked a ton of the end of the year, like, how are you going to operate your business, FD program, new kid, all the interclip stuff? Like, I'm just like, I'm the type of guy that's just like loaded up, you know, I might get through it. And I think just the motivation that keeps me going is that I'm able to do it. And I want to prove that I can do it and being able to like overcome whatever tasks is in front of me. I'm big on just mental performance, spend a lot of time and money on, on that stuff to get my mindset right. Um, and it trickles from, you know, business all the way down to FD. And it just, I walk in like, that's it. Like you, if you see me on grid, like I'm not the guy that's like out of my car, shooting the shit with every other driver right before we go on practice. Like I'm locked into my seat. I have everything, you know, I have my cool suit on. I have my earbuds in like I'm locked in and looking forward.
moments.why: His second kid arrived between rounds two and three of his rookie FD year.

moments.quote: Yeah, I think sleep is number one, but also I work with a sports psychologist. Oh, nice. So having my mindset, but more so keeping me level minded and like saying certain things to myself when I need to say things, then even to practice breathing, like that was something where I was never taught how to properly breathe. And I was like, it sounds so woo woo and dumb, but it is one of the most life -changing things you can learn.
moments.why: He works with a sports psychologist and calls learning to breathe life-changing.

moments.quote: Um, visualizing, like I visualize over and over and over again, the run, I visualize me winning the battle. I visualize the guy pointing to me, you got the win, like that type of stuff. And so when I do get in that position, I feel like I've already been there. And so all the, like I had no nerves whatsoever all year. And like, it's because I mentally prepared myself to be in that position, to be in that seat, especially with the SIM helping out of like literally seeing everything and knowing, okay, this is where I'm going to be.
moments.why: He visualizes winning every battle so he had zero nerves as an FD rookie.

moments.quote: Um, I mean, for us this year, just kind of finishing at the bottom, I think next year, like at a minimum, man, it's like, we have to be a top 10 competitive. Um, of course, like I'm going to tell you, like, we're going to be on the box every single round. Um, but like the realistic goals is just to have a car that is working a hundred percent, um, and just myself being comfortable behind the wheel with all the changes we made this year. Like I felt like I was driving someone else's car for the first three rounds. Like I'm just like, dude, this doesn't feel right. Um, you know, this isn't, this isn't my car. I don't feel comfortable. I'm not going to be able to perform at the level I can.
moments.why: After finishing at the bottom, his minimum goal for next year is top 10.

moments.quote: Uh, I'm just bummed out about how it all kind of panned out, but, uh, yeah, like the one round we, we had essentially like a car, uh, when we made it's top 16 and then, uh, Jerry Johnson took us out and top 16, which was, it was a pretty close battle, but it was a good battle. Everyone was like, Oh, I don't, I didn't know you could drive like that. I'm like, and so I think that's just a really big bummer, man. Like just like people truly think like what we did this year is like the level of my driving, which is like, yeah, embarrassing. Um, you know, but it's just like, again, man, it lights a fire in my butt. Like I cannot wait to get back out there.
moments.why: His one working weekend ended in Top 16 and people finally saw what he can do.

moments.quote: I, I will have my G out there for black Friday. I have a G sedan with the one J in it. And we just, uh, put a four door cage with four bucket seats. Oh, sick. Okay. Yeah. So I really wanted to build a car to like be able to just give ride alongs and, you know, share the experience of drifting. Uh, also give back to the partners that's kind of helped on the build. Um, and so yeah, we're going to be, uh, bringing that car out for black Friday. So super excited about that. And it should be a good time.
moments.why: He built a 1JZ G sedan with a four door cage to give ride-alongs at Black Friday.

episodes.title: At Gridlife Laguna

moments.quote: And arguably I would put, I would put it like, it's like ProSpec plus. That's like, I don't want to take away anything from ProSpec drivers. Cause I know how much goes into getting you there and like the amount of work that goes into that. But I personally feel like the competition or the level of the competition and the driving in hop it, I think it kind of tips the scale a little bit. moments.topic: ZERO POINTS FOR A LAZY ENTRY
moments.quote: So I'm doing a competition in Australia in Melbourne. First of it in in in Australia for a couple of years, which is kind of funny. And the guy running the competition said, let your imagination run wild and do whatever you want. It's sweet. I'm like you are opening Pandora's box. But so what I'm going to do for that particular competition as an experiment is use the initiation criteria of swings, so how much you swing in the body and the right of angle and giving a score on that. Yeah, so the plan is to set up a minimum amount of initiation aggression. We can call it. So if you don't meet a certain amount of swing and a certain amount of right to angle, you basically get a zero for your initiation. And we're going to do that at each point in the track. So effectively, when you transition, there'll be like a score and you will have to meet a certain amount of swing and a certain amount of right to angle to get points for that particular area.
moments.why: An Australian event will score initiation by body swing and rate to angle, with zero for weak entries.

moments.topic: A DASH GAUGE THAT GRADES YOUR FLICK
moments.quote: So this gauge is going to tether to the device that's on the roof of the car and it's going to give live feedback to the drivers on how their initiation and transitions are. Here it goes. You can see it raised that a lot. Look at that. So yeah, it does some cool things. But basically, this is going to be a live feedback gauge that's going to sit on the dash, tether to the device that's on your roof. Yeah, how you transition around the course is going to show up live immediately on that gauge. So you'll know if your initiation is not just is not just standard or if you're over transitioning like if you back it in, it's going to give you like another alert. So basically a training tool, but also a mechanism for drivers to get the perfect initiation and it's and it's chaseable. So yeah, the big conversation is right now is, you know, what is a chaseable and unchaseable initiation?
moments.why: Prototype dash gauge gives drivers live green/yellow/red feedback on initiations.
